claims.claim: Organizational culture is the shared values, beliefs, and norms that shape behavior in an organization; OpenStax's Principles of Management defines corporate culture as a culture based on the values the organization believes in, which motivate employees' beliefs, behaviors, relationships, and ways of working.

Culture has visible and invisible layers: Edgar Schein's model, as summarized in Lumen Learning's OER, describes three levels — artifacts (visible structures, processes, and signs), values (the stated 'why' behind how the company operates), and underlying assumptions (taken-for-granted beliefs and perceptions at the foundation).

Culture serves two crucial purposes for an organization: it helps the organization adapt to and integrate with its external environment, and it creates internal unity by bringing members together to work cohesively toward common goals.

Culture matters for decisions, retention, and performance: OpenStax calls organizational culture one of the most important internal dimensions of an organization's effectiveness criteria, and CFI lists turnover, employee morale, customer treatment, and customer satisfaction among the aspects of operations in which a company's culture is represented.

A strong culture rests on firmly regarded, broadly accepted ideas: employees understand how top management expects them to react in any circumstance, feel that response is the appropriate one, and understand they will be rewarded for embodying the company's values.

Larger organizations may host subcultures: different groupings of professionals (for example, hourly workers versus research scientists) can evolve different cultures even while the larger culture remains dominant.

Organizational cultures are generally framed and influenced by the top-level leader or founder, whose vision, values, and mission set the 'tone at the top' that models how other officers and employees work and behave.

Corporate culture is typically assumed rather than explicitly stated and evolves gradually over time as a result of the aggregate qualities of the people the company recruits; deliberate culture change requires revisiting core values, planning, and ongoing progress monitoring.
OpenStax describes culture as 'both the personality and glue that binds an organization' — the honest framing that culture is the organization's personality.

A strong culture is not automatically a good one: OpenStax's Amazon example shows a high-performing culture that was also criticized as a 'toxic cut-throat work environment,' so the lesson teaches strong = widely shared, not strong = healthy.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a strong culture is necessarily beneficial
positions: CFI describes strong culture as aligning employee responses and rewards with company values, framed as a success condition
OpenStax's Amazon example shows a strong, high-performing culture that was also criticized as a 'toxic cut-throat work environment'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines strong as widely shared and strongly held, not as good; a strong culture can carry healthy or harmful norms. Question 3 and the common-mistakes section teach this explicitly.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether culture can be deliberately changed or only evolves on its own
positions: CFI describes culture as typically assumed rather than stated and evolving gradually over time through the people an organization recruits
CFI also outlines deliberate steps senior management can take (revisiting values, setting culture goals, planning, monitoring progress)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are true: leaders can deliberately influence culture, but change is gradual and slow. The lesson teaches the honest note that culture shifts slowly, reinforced by Question 4.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 4.5: Corporate Cultures
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22 (openstax.org serves the page to a browser user-agent). Supports: culture as one of the most important internal dimensions of an organization's effectiveness; Peter Drucker's 'culture eats strategy for breakfast' as quoted by OpenStax; culture's two purposes (external adaptation, internal unity); culture as 'both the personality and glue that binds an organization'; cultures framed and influenced by the top-level leader or founder (tone at the top); the Competing Values Framework and its four culture types (adhocracy, clan, hierarchy, market, attributed to Cameron & Quinn 1999); subcultures within large organizations; the Amazon example showing a strong culture that was also criticized as toxic. Page footer states the book may not be ingested into LLMs without OpenStax's permission; used as reference only, no wording reproduced.
